planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated specimens in fall into undisturbed, well-drained, humus-rich soil over chalk or limestone, in dappled to full shade beneath beech or mixed deciduous canopy.

directions: White helleborine is a European woodland orchid of dense beech and mixed deciduous stands, forming upright spikes of creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers that barely open above glossy, sheathing leaves. It depends on an intact soil mycorrhizal network and thin leaf-litter ground cover rather than companion planting, so it establishes best when left undisturbed in shaded, calcareous, well-drained woodland soil. Growth is slow and plants may take several years to flower reliably after transplanting. Source only from reputable tissue-cultured stock, since wild collection damages fragile native populations.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated specimens in fall into calcareous, well-drained, humus-rich soil under an open deciduous or beech canopy with dappled light rather than deep gloom.

directions: This slender European orchid carries pure white flowers that open wider than its close relative white helleborine, held above narrow, sword-shaped leaves arranged up a wiry stem. It favors woodland rides, open coppice, and steep wooded banks where some filtered light reaches the ground, rather than the deepest shade, and is most often found over chalk or hard limestone. Like other Cephalanthera species it relies on a specific mycorrhizal partnership and resents root disturbance, so established plants should be left in place once sited. Enrich planting areas with leaf mold rather than conventional fertilizer.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated specimens in fall into free-draining, calcareous soil in dappled shade beneath beech or oak, ideally where some decaying deadwood is nearby.

directions: Red helleborine bears striking pink-purple flowers along a slender spike, mimicking bellflowers to attract pollinating bees that nest in nearby decaying wood rather than offering true nectar. It grows on free-draining, calcareous slopes in beech and oak woodland with sparse ground cover, avoiding both deep shade and open sun in favor of a dappled middle ground. This is one of the more demanding woodland orchids to establish, with populations that can fail to set seed for years even in the wild, so success depends on replicating undisturbed, humus-rich, lime-rich woodland soil and leaving the mycorrhizal relationship undisturbed. Best reserved for dedicated orchid collectors with suitable calcareous woodland conditions.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated specimens in fall into moist, neutral to mildly acidic, clay-rich woodland soil in dense shade beneath beech or mixed deciduous trees.

directions: Violet helleborine is among the most shade-tolerant of all terrestrial orchids, thriving in densely canopied beech woods where competing ground flora is sparse, and it has even increased in some regions as traditional woodland coppicing declined and shade deepened. Broad leaves tinged purple on their undersides line sturdy stems topped with pale green, white-lipped flowers that open in mid- to late summer, later than most other woodland orchids. It prefers neutral to mildly acidic, clay-rich soil that stays reliably moist and benefits from an undisturbed leaf-litter layer. As with related Epipactis species, avoid cultivating soil around the base once established, since the roots and their fungal partners are easily damaged.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers about 3 inches deep in fall into moist, humus-rich loam over chalk or limestone, at woodland edges or recently coppiced areas with dappled shade.

directions: Early purple orchid produces dense spikes of rich purple flowers above leaves often marked with dark purple blotches, appearing from early to mid spring in deciduous woodland edges, recently coppiced glades, and unimproved grassland alike. It favors dappled rather than deep shade, since it needs more light than true deep-woodland orchids but still benefits from the moisture and leaf mold that tree cover provides. Soil should stay consistently moist and humus-rich without waterlogging, ideally over chalk or limestone bedrock. Avoid any fertilizer or fungicide near the planting site, as both can disrupt the orchid's essential mycorrhizal fungus, and leave established clumps undisturbed once they take hold.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers in fall into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil over chalk or limestone, in the dappled shade of open deciduous woodland or scrub edges.

directions: Lady orchid is one of the most imposing European woodland orchids, sending up a tall, dense spike of maroon-hooded, pale-lipped flowers from a basal rosette of broad, glossy leaves in late spring. It grows naturally in sloping, partially shaded deciduous or mixed woodland over chalk or limestone, favoring dappled light filtering through hazel, beech, or ash rather than open ground or heavy shade. Keep the humus-rich soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, and avoid disturbing the root zone once plants are established, since the tubers and their fungal partnership are easily damaged. This is a specialist plant best suited to collectors who can provide calcareous, well-drained woodland conditions.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers in fall into gritty, free-draining, calcareous soil in mid-shade to full sun, such as the edge of hazel-ash woodland or a limestone rock garden.

directions: Dense-flowered orchid is a diminutive, unusually adaptable species that tolerates both open limestone grassland and the mid-shade of hazel-ash woodland, where it sends up a short, tightly packed spike of tiny, vanilla-scented, white-to-pink flowers in spring. It needs sharply drained, calcareous or slightly acidic gritty soil and resents sitting wet over winter. Because it is naturally rare and declining in parts of its range, only plant nursery-propagated stock, and site it where competing vegetation stays sparse so the small rosette of leaves is not overwhelmed. Leave established plants undisturbed, since like most terrestrial orchids it depends on an intact mycorrhizal partnership in the soil.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland

planting.note: Plant rhizomes horizontally a couple of inches deep in fall into moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees; mark the site, as the plant disappears completely by early summer.

directions: This naturally occurring hybrid between wood anemone and yellow wood anemone combines the familiar spreading, rhizomatous habit and deeply divided foliage of its parents with soft, buttery pale-yellow flowers that bridge the cool white and warm gold of the two species. Like both parents it is a true spring ephemeral, flowering in early spring before tree canopy closes and dying back completely to the rhizome by early summer, so companion plantings should fill the gap it leaves behind. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial shade, where it slowly forms expanding colonies over the years. It combines well with the white and blue tones of other spring woodland bulbs.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into evenly moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; keep soil from drying out through summer.

directions: Banana Boat is a golden-leaved selection of the Japanese and Korean woodland sedge Carex siderosticta, carrying broad, banana-yellow, grass-unlike blades edged and lightly streaked in green on arching, wiry stems. It spreads gradually by rhizomes to form a dense, deciduous groundcover mat under trees, brightening shaded borders where little else keeps its color so consistently. Unlike many ornamental sedges it tolerates close to full shade well, though it needs steady moisture through the growing season and will scorch if allowed to dry out during summer heat. Divide congested patches in spring every few years to maintain vigor and control spread.

planting.note: Plant small tubers shallowly in fall into gritty, sharply drained, humus-rich soil in part sun to light shade, sheltered from wind under trees or large rocks; protect from hard freezes in colder zones.

directions: Cyprus cyclamen is a small, tender woodland species native only to Cyprus, producing intensely fragrant, pale pink flowers from fall into early winter, followed by heart-shaped leaves marbled in silver and pale green that persist through winter before the plant goes dormant in spring. It needs the sheltered understory conditions of trees, shrubs, or large rocks, since it dislikes exposure to wind, and sharply drained, gritty soil that never stays wet. Because it is among the least cold-hardy of the hardy cyclamen group, it is best grown in warm-winter gardens or containers that can be moved under cover where temperatures drop much below freezing. Keep tubers on the dry side through their spring-to-summer dormancy.
